abstract:
A study identified increased levels of the enzyme EPHX1 in the livers of mice and patients with advanced fibrosis and showed that EPHXI promotes liver fibrosis by decreasing EET levels.

The post Metabolic Pathway Identified as Potential Target for Liver Diseases appeared first on GEN - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News.

metadata.author: Sophia Ktori

content.value:
Dietary polyunsaturated fats are converted into metabolites via metabolic pathways. One such pathway involves the production of the metabolite epoxyeicosatrienoic acid (EET), which has anti-inflammatory and protective effects in the liver.

However, some EETs are converted into dihydroxyeicosatrienoic acids (DHETs) by enzymes, reducing their beneficial effects and potentially contributing to the progression of diseases like fibrosis into its more severe form, cirrhosis.

A study led by Hiroko Ikenaga, MD, PhD, and Associate Professor Tsutomu Matsubara, PhD, at the Graduate School of Medicine, Osaka Metropolitan University, now found increased levels of the enzyme hepatic microsomal epoxide hydrolase EPHX1 in the livers of mice and patients with advanced fibrosis, and showed that EPHXI promotes liver fibrosis by decreasing EET levels. The enzyme was associated with decreased levels of a specific EET (11,12-EET) and increased levels of its corresponding DHET (11,12-DHET).

Mice bred to lack EPHX1 showed increased 11,12-EET levels and less generation of fibers and oxidative stress associated with advanced forms of fibrosis. The researchers reported their findings in JCI Insight, in a paper titled “Hepatic EPHX1 Potentiates Liver Fibrosis by Decreasing Eicosatrienoic Acids,” in which they concluded, “This study provides evidence that EPHX1 contributes to EET hydrolysis in the liver and participates in liver fibrogenesis, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic target.”

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a chronic liver disease that affects approximately 25% of the world population, with prevalence expected to increase,” the authors explained. “MASLD causes liver fibrosis, particularly in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), and can lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.”

Lipidome analysis has identified lipid metabolites, including saturated fatty acids, free cholesterol, phospholipids, and polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), as clinical biomarkers of MASLD in humans, they continued. “Among them, PUFA-derived metabolites exert diverse and biologically potent effects in MASLD … lipid metabolites, especially PUFA metabolites, are thought to be associated with MASLD pathogenesis and progression.”

There have been few lipidomic studies evaluating the effects of PUFA metabolites on liver fibrosis by comprehensively analyzing clinical specimens, animals and cells, however, and the effects of PUFA metabolites on liver fibrosis isn’t well understood.

To help better understand the role of EET, the researchers treated liver cells called hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) with 11,12-EET. They found that these treated cells showed reduced oxidative stress and suppressed transforming growth factor-β-induced HSC activation, which are important in reducing the progression of fibrosis. “Ephx1-null mice showed attenuation of EET hydrolysis, oxidative stress, and fibrogenesis in the livers …” the authors further noted.

“Both suppressing EPHX1 activity or preserving and restoring 11,12-EET activity represent promising therapeutic strategies for liver fibrosis,” Ikenaga suggested.

The findings may also help to identify patients at risk of the more severe forms of liver fibrosis. Tracking levels of 11,12-DHET in blood samples may serve as a biomarker for more severe liver fibrosis.

Such biomarkers are useful for investigating changes in the bodies of patients that can help identify those in need of treatment before their condition worsens. In fibrosis, this could be the difference between stopping disease progression early and it becoming more severe conditions like cirrhosis or liver failure.

In conclusion, the authors noted, their study findings demonstrate that EPHX1 promotes hepatic fibrogenesis through dysregulation of EET metabolism. “Enhanced hepatic EPHX1 expression facilitates the hydrolysis of EETs into DHETs and can lead to liver fibrosis, resulting in increased serum DHET levels, which are indicators for advanced liver fibrosis. Targeting the EET metabolic pathway may provide a therapeutic strategy for liver fibrosis.”

While both EPHX1 and 11,12-EET show promise for therapeutics development, there are challenges, the authors acknowledge. “There is currently a lack of drugs that inhibit EPHX1 in humans and those that affect 11,12-EET are unstable,” Matsubara said. “Many challenges remain before clinical application becomes possible, not only in developing compounds that act stably within the body but also verifying their safety. Our hope is that these findings act as a basis for accelerating the development of new therapies, especially those targeting EPHX1, for the treatment of liver diseases like fibrosis and cirrhosis.”
